result.weather: A front has moved through: wind speed and direction over the hotspots differ from calibration. Drag, shear, veer and updraft are unchanged. Use measure_wind.

notes.text: I'm starting by reading the mission briefing to get oriented before doing anything else.

I'm working out how to estimate the wind and drag from the data: wind speed, direction, and shear and veer can come straight from readings taken at different altitudes, while drag has to be inferred from impact. I also want to use the smoke drops to check for updrafts, and during operation I can take wind readings at several altitudes to track speed and direction again.

Next I'll run four drops at altitudes of 30, 60, 100, and 150 meters, kept well away from the smoke, to build the wind profile and get a handle on drag. Fall time and horizontal travel should reveal drag, since a higher drag coefficient means a slower terminal velocity and a longer fall. Once those are in, I'll move on to drops through the smoke column to check for updrafts.

Now I'm comparing wind speeds at 40, 100, and 150 meters, and the shear exponents I get from the log ratios come out around 0.12 between 100 and 150 and 0.35 between 40 and 100. Given the roughly 0.5 m/s noise, I'm estimating a combined shear somewhere near 0.25 to 0.3, and I'm starting to look at how the wind direction veers from 40 to 150 meters.

Now I'm working through the drag problem: a drop from 100 m takes 7.13 s, while the vacuum fall time would be about 4.52 s, so drag is clearly significant. I'm testing a drag hypothesis with a quadratic model and considering how the horizontal velocity couples into the vertical fall.

The predicted fall times run long, so the drag must be a bit lower. I'll try 0.027. Every test points the same way: the predicted travel is short in each direction, which means the drag is too high. I'll try 0.026 next.

I'm narrowing the drag coefficient down to about 0.0274 from three test runs, and now I need to turn to the wind profile, which still needs more data.

I'm planning seven more test drops, with the aim of catching an updraft by releasing from 150 m so the load drifts down through the smoke column near the center. I'm also weighing how readings at 30, 70, 120 and 150 m would pin down the wind profile, since shear and veer show up in how far each drop drifts.

I'm settling on a design for the smoke drop: release from 150 m, heading 90, at about 45 m/s, with an offset in y to compensate for the wind's northward drift, so the load passes through the updraft column near the center. Before committing, I want to run a simulation to check the landing point.

I'm shifting the release point by roughly (-16, -9.4) to account for the updraft, which puts the drop at (-101, -49). Since the updraft is unknown, the landing will differ, but comparing results will reveal its effect. I want the impact to be sensitive to the updraft, since slower descent means more wind drift and more time spent moving horizontally. I'll run the test drop at (-101, -49) and simultaneously run additional drops at altitudes 30, 70, and 120 to measure the wind.

I'll also run another smoke drop with different geometry, at low altitude 60 heading 0. For now I'm doing the first smoke drop alongside the wind drops at 30 and 120, which carry no smoke.

I'm pulling the wind speed readings at each height, then setting up a power-law fit by taking logs of speed and of height relative to 100 m.

Now I'm working out the regression for the log-log fit, then the wind shear and intercept, and I'm also setting up a linear fit of direction against height.

The regression gives a direction slope of about -19.6 degrees per 100 m, with the fitted direction at 100 m near 37 degrees, a few degrees off the measured 32, which I'll treat as noise. That puts the working hypothesis at wind speed 5.95, direction 37, shear 0.33, veer -19.6, and drag 0.0274. Next I'll pull the updraft from test 4 and compare it against updraft 5 first.

The test 4 result is a bit off in the opposite direction from what more updraft would suggest: the shorter predicted fall would mean a slightly larger updraft, but a longer time aloft would push the drift further north. I'll test the updraft at 7 and 3 to see how sensitive the result is.

The updraft estimate works out to about 5.35, with the sensitivity of fall time to wind speed at roughly 0.35 s per m/s. Since hotspot intensities go up to 1.4 and the fall-time noise is 0.05 s, the updraft accuracy should land around 0.15.

I'm going to run another smoke drop at altitude 80 with heading 0, since test 4 was the only one that pinned down drag and I want more data to separate it from the updraft estimate. Precision matters here because the score drops off with distance, so I'm checking that the wind error from 20 noisy readings stays around a metre of drift.

I'm weighing two more smoke drops: one at 60 m heading 180 to cross the column, and one at 100 m heading 300. I'm estimating the low-altitude drop from test 3, which drifted about 55 m south, and expecting roughly 70 m of travel once the updraft slows the fall. The misfit across the six tests is small, within about twice the measurement noise, so I'll leave the model as it is and just add the drops.

I'm still working out where to drop the next smoke test so the release point lands near the center, and I'm noting that I have about 115 calculations to spend.

I'm shifting the release point by (-6.3, -24.5) to (-16.3, 50.5), which still puts it inside the column top, and the trajectory should cross the axis from there. I'll do that one, and I'm also weighing a separate non-smoke drop at 70 m for wind readings, though those readings may already come from the smoke drop. Next I'm looking at the other run at heading 300, altitude 110, speed 65.

I'm working out the predicted fall time. The simulation gave about 6.17 for the shifted release, but since the trajectory now passes closer to the center, that estimate may not hold. The observed time was 7.01, so I'll compare the two.

I'm looking at test 7 with dt at -0.22 and wondering whether the updraft needs to be stronger. Test 4 points to about 5.35, which conflicts with that, so the updraft's shape over time might be the explanation. Test 7 also seems to pass more through the center at low altitude, so it spends more time in the column, but I don't know how sensitive it is. I'll try an updraft of 6.

Checking the updraft numbers from Test 7 and Test 4 against each other, they disagree by about 0.55 m/s, which is far more than the 0.15 m/s per test that the timing noise could explain. Drag seems like the likelier culprit, since it would shift both tests, and I'm about to look at how the non-smoke runs drop dt.

Now I'm comparing the non-smoke drops: the early tests sit near zero, while tests 5 and 6 come out about 0.08 and 0.11 s later, which might mean drag is lower than I assumed. The position offsets also look systematic: tests 4 and 6 land northeast of where the model predicts, which points toward too much wind drift or too strong an updraft at altitude.

I'm checking whether the residuals point to drag or to measurement noise. The heading and speed pattern doesn't line up cleanly with drag alone, so I'm considering impact noise of about 1.5 m per axis as a possible explanation.

Working through the residuals, the miss distance of about 2.1 m sits within what impact noise would explain, so the model holds up. The updraft mismatch is still about 0.2 s, which looks too large for timing noise alone. I'm going to test lower drag together with a higher updraft of 5.7 to see if that resolves both tests.

I'm still seeing test 7 at -0.14 and test 4 at +0.02, so the relative gap stays around 0.16 to 0.2. My guess is that test 7's path doesn't cross the axis exactly as the model assumes, since its lateral offset within the column matters. Its release point is just outside the column, and the model-predicted and observed impacts still come out nearly the same. Hmm, what about the min

I'm checking whether test 4's path, entering the column around x=-50 and spending a long time inside it, could explain the gap, and whether shear at low altitude might shift test 7's position. Both feel like weak explanations. The 0.16 s discrepancy works out to about a 0.45 m/s updraft difference, which would only move the impact by roughly a meter, so it's probably acceptable for the operation. Using the remaining drops for another smoke run or more wind readings at different altitudes might settle it.

I'm weighing whether the remaining drops are better spent on drag and updraft or on wind readings, and I'm leaning toward test drops, since measure_wind can already capture shear and veer during the operation itself. I'm planning one smoke drop at 120 m heading 270 at speed 55, aimed near the center, and a low-altitude one at 40 m heading 45 at speed 45, then simulating both to place them.

I'm adjusting the first point by releasing it from (80, -40) with a small offset, landing at about (46.7, -32.1), though the column entry looks different from what I expected since it starts just outside the column at r=57. I'll accept that and move on to the second adjustment, which comes out to (-54.9, -53.3).

I'm comparing test 8 and test 4: both are high, but test 8 heads west against the wind while test 4 heads east with it, so the wind direction might explain the gap. The fall-time difference also seems to point to more updraft. I suspect the wind model itself is off.

I'm weighing whether westward travel against the wind would mean more drag, but the longer fall and further westward landing point the other way. I'm redoing the wind fit with all nine readings, transforming heights and speeds logarithmically to get the averages I need.

I'm running the weighted fit over the nine readings: the log-transformed heights and speeds give a shear of about 0.31, which puts the surface wind near 5.9. Now I'm turning to the direction readings at each height.

I'm computing the direction fit now: the mean height and direction come out near 91 and 37, and the deviations give a negative cross-product sum. That works out to a slope of about -0.17, so the wind veers by roughly 16.5 degrees across the heights.

I'm pinning down the direction at 100 metres, which comes out near 35.75 degrees after the veer adjustment. With the wind at about 5.9, a direction of roughly 36, shear of 0.31 and veer of -16.5, the next step is to fit the drag and updraft parameters, and rather than tuning them by hand against residuals, I'll try a direct fit.

I'm checking test 8, which is still off by -0.27 in dt, while the smoke-related tests show mixed offsets and the nonsmoke runs look fine. I'm now wondering whether the trajectory passing off-axis relative to the real path could explain the discrepancy for that release point.

I'm checking whether test 8's lateral position along the path, around y≈-30, puts it close enough to the axis to change the updraft it sees. Since the model already matches the impact y, I'm wondering if a slightly more northward real path would explain the gap, though drag changes would likely break the nonsmoke runs. I'm considering raising the updraft to around 6.5 to fit tests 7 through 9, and I'm not yet sure how test 8 will respond.

I'm working out the sensitivity for test 8 and then estimating the target value from each test's own data, starting with test 8 alone, then tests 7, 4, and 9, before combining them with a weighting by sensitivity squared.

Now I'm checking the weighted mean against the residuals for each test. Test 4 sits about 2.4σ off, which is borderline, and I'm considering whether a small drag adjustment for that high, slow drop would bring it in line. The positional residuals are bigger than the noise: test 4 lands about 3 units north of where it actually fell, and test 8 about 3.8 units east. I'm wondering whether weaker or differently directed wind at mid altitudes would explain both at once.

Checking whether the NE drift explanation holds: test 2 and test 6 are long nonsmoke falls but don't drift strongly NE, so a simple wind reduction doesn't clearly account for the smoke-drop residuals. I'm wondering whether the extra time the load spends aloft in the updraft is what's driving the extra drift.

I'm noticing that the two smoke drops pull in opposite directions under a drag change: test 4 heading east would need more drag, and test 8 heading west would need less, so a drag tweak can't fix both. Both residuals point to the predicted path running too far east, which suggests the wind's eastward component is overstated rather than the drag being wrong.

Now I'm checking the overall residuals across all nine tests. The nonsmoke drops don't show the same northeast pattern, so a simple wind reduction doesn't fully explain things. Averaging the x and y residuals gives a small eastward and northward bias, which points back toward the wind's eastward component being somewhat overstated.

I'm weighing whether the remaining residuals of 3–4 m on tests 4 and 8 are just noise or a real pattern, since both are smoke drops. The fact that both sit in the column makes me suspect the updraft or drag, and that matters for where to drop. Dropping at a lower altitude would cut the time spent in the column, which should limit errors like these.

I'm going to try a joint adjustment to drag and updraft, aiming to cut the drift in tests 4 and 8 without disturbing the others. Shifting the wind at mid altitudes would help one test but not both, so I'm looking at what changes the slow, long-time descent through the column.

I'm going to test a couple of joint variants next, starting with a slightly higher drag and updraft, to see whether that cuts the drift in tests 4 and 8 without throwing off the others.

The drag estimate of about 0.027 holds up, and since drag shifts position noticeably, an error of 0.0003 would already cost roughly half a metre. I'm going back to drag 0.027 and updraft 6.1, and now I'll test wind tweaks, starting with wind speed 5.6 and shear 0.31 to compare against the baseline.

I'm working out the mean residuals across the nine points: about -0.68 in x and -0.98 in y, so the prediction runs slightly too far southwest on average. Next I'm estimating how much the wind-speed term shifts that per meter per second.

I'm checking how a wind-speed change of about -0.26 m/s would move the predicted position, which comes out around -0.8 in x and -1.2 in y per step. The mean residual leans the other way, so the best wind speed is probably near 5.8. Two tests disagree, though: one wants more wind at higher altitude and the other wants less, so the smoke condition may be what's changing the picture.

I'm wondering whether the wind-speed fit is being pulled off course by noise: the test 8 x-residual of 3.1 is about two sigma, which could easily be chance. The residual directions are scattered, so there may not be one clean wind-driven explanation here.

I'm settling on a drag value of about 0.027 and an updraft near 6.1, since those matter most for the operation. I'm now trying to refine the drag estimate using the nonsmoke time-of-flight residuals, which average slightly positive.

I'm settling on a drag value near 0.027, since the nonsmoke time-of-flight residuals point to something slightly lower, around 0.0268, while the different test groups pull in opposite directions. Rather than spend the last test on a guess, I'll use it on another high-altitude smoke drop heading north at speed 60 to check the updraft and drift before running the operation.

I'm planning to settle the 4/8 discrepancy with the remaining test drop, simulating a high-altitude smoke drop with drag 0.027, wind speed 5.75, and updraft 6.1.

I'm folding in the new wind reading of 6.8 at 28 for the 140 point, which adds ln values of 0.336 and 1.917 to the fit. Shear should rise a little, so I'm recomputing the sums and means quickly, starting with the x and y totals for all ten points.

Still crunching the cross-products and sums of squares for the regression...

Checking the variance totals and the veer, then comparing the wind speed, direction, shear and drag against the compromise values.

I'm checking test 10's timestep, which looks fine, and noting its position at (2.5, 1.5). Several smoke drops seem to show a positive residual in the NE direction, including tests 4, 8, 10, 7 and 9.

Checking whether the smoke drops' northeast residual comes from the updraft. A larger updraft would make the fall longer and drift more, which is the wrong direction, so that doesn't explain it. I'm also weighing whether the updraft changes the relative airspeed enough to bleed off horizontal drift faster, though the model may already cover that. Comparing the average smoke-drop residual, around 2.5 m to the northeast, against the non-smoke average near zero, the gap is roughly 3 m.

I'm comparing the smoke-drop residuals with the non-smoke ones, and the longer smoke falls don't seem to explain the gap by themselves. I'm wondering whether drag or wind strength might be the cause, since test 8's westward miss points toward lower drag or weaker easterly wind.

I'm settling on the wind as the likely cause: the extra drift is about 2.5 m over roughly 8 s, which points to around 0.3 m/s less wind for the smoke drops, while the non-smoke ones would want a bit more. I'm also wondering whether the updraft, by stretching the time aloft, could be shifting how the wind acts on the load at lower altitudes.

I'm testing whether a lower drag with a stronger updraft could fit, but that would speed up the non-smoke falls and push the eastward and northward misses the wrong way, so I'm dropping that idea. I'll accept a 2-3 m error on the high smoke drops and lean on the low-altitude ones, which fit within about 1.5 m, since in operation the wind is measured directly.

Settling on a final calibration set: drag 0.027, shear 0.32, veer -16.8, updraft 6.1, and I'll start from there.

Starting the operation with the calibrated set now.

I'm planning the wind measurements: taking 20 readings across altitudes from 30 to 150, with extra weight near 100. I'll start with a first batch of 10 readings spread across 30, 60, 100, 130, and 150, each taken twice.

I'm estimating wind speed and direction at 100 m from all the readings, using the known shear and veer from calibration. Each reading gets normalized to 100 m by dividing by the shear factor, and I'm working through the 30 m values first, which come out to about 6.8 and 7.2.

I'm checking the normalized speeds at 100 m, which average a bit lower than I'd expect. Next I'm working through the direction values and their mean, then planning to collect 12 more readings concentrated around 40 to 140 m.

I'm deciding to use all 12 remaining readings now rather than holding any back.

I'm fitting all 20 readings now, and wondering whether shear and veer should be fit jointly across both datasets. I'll start by fitting only the new data, then combine the results afterward.

I'm working through the group averages for each depth, then converting the positions and mean speeds to logs so I can weight the fit by the number of readings in each group.

Still computing the weighted sums...

I'm getting a shear estimate of about 0.253 from the new data, and the calibration run gave 0.318. The uncertainty on the new-data shear is roughly 0.035, based on per-reading noise and the spread of depths.

Now I'm working out the veer from the new data, starting with the mean depth and mean position, then the deviations and their cross-products.

Now I'm comparing the new-data veer against the calibration value, which differs by about 6 degrees, so I need to combine them.

Now I'm checking whether the combined shear of about 0.275 and veer of about -20.4 still hold up when I refit the calibration run with those values, since the shift from the calibration estimates is small but worth confirming.

I'm recomputing the calibration intercept with the combined shear of 0.275, which gives a wind speed of about 5.85 at 100 m. Using the veer of -20.4, the direction at 100 m works out to roughly 35.5 degrees. Next I'm comparing these refit values against the drag of 0.027 and the updraft of 6.1.

I'm checking the mean displacements across the ten points, which work out to about 0.6 in x and 0.11 in y, and that looks fine. Next I'm moving on to the updraft fine-tuning for the smoke.

Still working through the wind normalization, converting each speed with the shear factor to compare the levels on a common basis.

Now I'm averaging the normalized speeds across the levels to get a reference value, and the totals come out to a mean of about 6.48.

I've got the corrected wind fit now: drag 0.027, ground speed 6.48, direction about 62.5, with shear 0.275 and veer -20.4. Next I'm picking each target's altitude at the low end of its range, since that means less fall time and less error, and a mid-range heading, then simulating from a guessed release point and correcting iteratively.

Now I'm choosing the altitude for each target, working toward the lowest end of its range to shorten fall time and cut wind error, and then simulating from a guessed release point to correct the impact offset.

I'm setting each target's altitude near the bottom of its range and choosing a heading in the middle, starting with target 1 at about 108 m on a 342° heading with a speed of roughly 49.5. I'm going through the other four targets the same way, keeping the chosen altitudes, headings and speeds for each. I also want to check whether the simulation should include the target fire's own column, and I'm leaning toward yes, since I'll run the simulations next.

Now I'm running the first simulations with each release point placed directly over its target.

I'm working out the offsets for each tree, checking how much the updraft has already shifted each release point inside the column.

Now I'm finishing the offset for the last tree, which brings the updraft shift on its release point to the same scale as the others.

I'm going through the per-target errors, with T1 and T2 already resolved and T3 to T5 still pending.

I'm noting that the corrections may not scale linearly, since deeper into the column there's more updraft, so I'll need to iterate again.

Checking the residuals: the T1, T2 and T4 errors are small and fine. For T3, I'm estimating the release adjustment from the observed impact change, which comes out to a local gain of about 1.24, so I'm dividing the residual by that gain to get a corrected release of roughly (1138.95, -951.34).

I'm checking whether the smoke-drop bias points along the wind: the high-altitude drops average about (2.3, 1.3), which is roughly 60° against a 36° wind, so it's only loosely downwind and the evidence for a systematic offset is modest.

I'm weighing whether the high-altitude smoke drops reflect a real parameter error rather than noise: their mean offset is about 2.6 m, roughly downwind, and the three-drop average is moderately significant. I could test whether a shifted calibration (lower wind speed, more shear) would fit them better without breaking the others, though the measured operational wind makes that only partly useful.

I'm considering whether the updraft could explain the smaller horizontal drift: if the load spent its time at lower altitudes, where the wind is weaker, that would shorten the drift without changing the fall time.

I'm wondering whether a larger drag or a stronger updraft could shorten the horizontal drift without changing the fall time, but the drag change already caused large errors on the non-smoke tests, so drag looks like the dominant error. Test 2 at the same altitude fits well and even pulls slightly north, which makes a single shear or wind-speed tweak hard to justify from these residuals alone.

I'm comparing tests 2 and 4, which sit at the same altitude but differ by about 4.6 m in the y direction, and the only real difference between them is the smoke and the speed. The model's extra northward drift over the roughly one extra second of fall doesn't match the real data, where the fall time is longer but the drift is smaller, so something other than the updraft is probably shaping the horizontal result.

I'm testing whether a higher updraft paired with lower drag could close the gap, but the earlier run at drag 0.026 already showed the fall times coming out too short, so that combination doesn't hold up.

I'm going to try a couple of compares that vary shear and veer, since those carry over to operation, to see whether the smoke residuals shrink without breaking the others. I'll start with a lower wind speed and stronger shear, and keep the pragmatic fallback in mind: if the bias is real, it's roughly 2.6 m in the wrong direction, which costs about 0.2 in score.

I'm weighing a half correction of about 1.3 m toward upwind for the high smoke drops, since that hedges the bias either way. The open question is whether the bias is fixed to geography or tied to the wind: the tests at east, west and north all leaned northeast, which points toward the wind rather than the heading. If that holds, the offset in operation would sit roughly 24° clockwise from the new wind direction of about 62°.

I'm settling on a bias direction of roughly 70°, since the wind and the smoke offset seem to line up. I'm also checking whether the size of the bias tracks the extra fall time from the updraft, though the calibration and operation cases don't give a clean relationship.

I'm considering a slightly lower wind speed with a bit more shear, or a small drag and updraft adjustment, but those earlier runs already showed the drag change hurting the non-smoke tests. I'll try one comparison with a weaker wind speed to see whether the smoke drops respond more strongly than the others.

I'm considering a modest hedge: shifting the aim about 1 to 1.5 m upwind to offset the likely bias, since three high-altitude smoke drops show roughly 2.6 m of offset and test 2 pulls the other way, so the evidence is real but noisy.

I'm deciding to shift the release about 1 m downwind, toward roughly 65°, since the smoke bias is more likely real than not. That would apply to the high, low-intensity drops T1, T3 and T5, and possibly T2.

Working thro

I'm weighing whether to check how sensitive the result is to the shear and veer values, and whether a refit wind would change predictions much. I'm about to test T3 with shear 0.253 and veer -22.9, refitting the wind speed and direction to match.

I'm working out the wind speed and direction for T3 from the refit with shear 0.253 and veer -22.9, which comes to about 6.45 and 62.2. Next I'll run the T3 baseline simulation with those values.
Settling the remaining shifts now, and I'm going back over the hedge shift one more time before committing to it.
